title: Line-Skip Passes: Flash Pass, Fast Lane, Quick Queue
h1: Line-skip passes at ten parks: what Flash Pass, Fast Lane and Quick Queue cost and when they are worth it
metaDescription: THE FLASH Pass at Six Flags, Fast Lane at Knott's and Quick Queue at SeaWorld, priced and compared: which tier to buy, when to skip buying, and the Legoland honest answer.
summary: Four park companies sell four different line-skip products, and none of them work at the others. This guide prices THE FLASH Pass, Fast Lane and Quick Queue as of July 2026, names the tier worth buying at each park, and gives the Legolands the honest nothing-to-buy answer.
intro: This site covers ten parks run by four different companies, and every one of the big three companies sells a paid line-skip product with a different name, a different tier structure and a different pricing philosophy. Six Flags sells THE FLASH Pass. Knott's (Cedar Fair) sells Fast Lane. The SeaWorld parks (United Parks) sell Quick Queue. The Legolands sell no comparable product at all, which is itself the answer to a question families ask constantly.

The general rule across all of them: the product is priced like the crowd it is escaping. A quiet spring weekday makes every tier a waste of money; a July Saturday or a peak haunt night makes even the top tier look reasonable. Buy the day, not the brand — and check the specific park's pricing page before committing, because every figure below is a range, dated, and dynamic.

One more rule that matters more here than on either sister site: no product crosses companies. A FLASH Pass does nothing at Knott's, Fast Lane does nothing at SeaWorld, and nothing you can buy works at the Legolands. Multi-park trips need multi-park arithmetic.
keyPoints: Six Flags THE FLASH Pass is sold at all four Six Flags parks here, in tiers that change the discount depth, not the ride list.
Knott's Fast Lane covers the headliners on one wristband; the premium tier adds the newest rides.
SeaWorld Quick Queue is tiered by ride coverage, and the Orlando park has the most coasters worth skipping onto.
The Legolands sell no line-skip product — their queues are managed by timing instead, and that is the honest answer.
Weekday visitors almost never need any of these. The peak-crowd days these products are built for are the days they cost the most.
Prices are ranges as of July 2026 and move with demand — always confirm the park's own page on the day you buy.

sections.heading: What these products actually are
body: All three products are the same idea wearing three uniforms: pay extra, join a shorter queue at participating rides, and repeat through the day. The mechanics differ in ways that matter at the margin — Six Flags' device-based reservations, Knott's one-price wristband, SeaWorld's ride-tiered bands — but the purchase question is identical everywhere: how much of your day is queueing, and what is removing half of it worth?

None of these products is a front-of-line guarantee in every case. All three reserve the right to exclude specific rides (usually the newest or the highest-capacity), and all three get scarcer on peak days. The list of excluded rides is on each park's product page, and it is the one detail worth checking before buying.

list.title: The three products at a glance
items: THE FLASH Pass — Six Flags parks (Magic Mountain, Over Texas, Great Adventure, Great America). Device- or app-based reservation system with tiered discount depth.
Fast Lane — Knott's Berry Farm. One-price wristband, unlimited use on the covered ride list, premium tier adds headliners.
Quick Queue — SeaWorld parks (San Diego, San Antonio, Orlando). Tiered bands by ride coverage; the top tiers add the biggest coasters.
No product — both Legolands. Queues are short enough that the parks sell timing advice instead, effectively.

sections.heading: THE FLASH Pass at the Six Flags parks
body: Six Flags' product is the most complicated of the three because its tiers change how the reservation system behaves rather than which rides you may skip. The base tier schedules one ride at a time with wait-discounted return windows; the middle tier discounts the waits further and allows more flexible re-riding; the top tier behaves closest to unlimited front-of-line. The price spread between the tiers is wide, and the park prices all of them by date.

At the four Six Flags parks on this site, the honest tier advice is consistent: on a weekday, buy nothing; on a regular summer weekend, the middle tier is usually the value point; on a peak haunt-season Saturday at Great Adventure or Great America, the top tier is the only one that meaningfully changes the day, and it is priced accordingly. As of July 2026, expect roughly the $40–70 range for base tiers on regular days and well into the hundreds for top tiers on peak dates at the big parks — confirm the live figure on the park's page.

The trap at Six Flags is buying any tier on a day that does not need it. Weekday operation at these parks runs thin enough that the standby queue for most headliners is under thirty minutes all day, and no reservation system beats a short line you can see.

sections.heading: Fast Lane at Knott's
body: Knott's Fast Lane is the simplest product of the three: one wristband, one price, unlimited use on the covered ride list for the day. The premium tier (Fast Lane Plus historically) adds the newest and most popular rides to the list — at Knott's that has meant the headliners like HangTime and GhostRider. The wristband mechanics mean no reservations to manage, which families consistently rate as the least stressful version of this purchase.

The value question at Knott's is sharper than at the Six Flags parks because the park is compact: walking between the covered rides is minutes, so a Fast Lane day can genuinely run the full headliner list twice before dinner. On the day types that need it — summer weekends and the fall haunt-adjacent days — it is the most efficient product per dollar on this site. As of July 2026, expect the mid-$100s for the base wristband on peak days, with the premium tier above that; the park's page has the live figure.

October needs its own paragraph: on fall haunt nights the day park closes early and the event itself is separately ticketed. Fast Lane is a day-product; buy it for the family Saturday, not the haunt Saturday.

sections.heading: Quick Queue at the SeaWorld parks
body: SeaWorld's Quick Queue is tiered by ride coverage: the base band covers a subset of attractions, and the top tiers add the biggest coasters. At Orlando — five real coasters including Mako and Kraken — the top tier is one of the most transformative products on this site, because the park's headline queue problem is concentrated in exactly the rides the top tier covers. At San Diego and San Antonio the lineup is smaller and the lower tiers usually suffice.

The show-schedule interaction is the SeaWorld-specific trick: every park on this site tells you the queues dip during the stadium presentations, and at the SeaWorld parks that is doubly true. A Quick Queue purchase plus deliberate show-timing can produce a near-walk-on coaster day at a fraction of the top-tier price — the crowd is in the stadium, not the queue.

As of July 2026, expect the base tiers from roughly $60–80 at the SeaWorld parks and the top tiers above $100 on peak dates, highest at Orlando. Confirm the live figure and the covered-ride list on each park's page — the tier boundaries move with new ride openings.

list.title: Quick Queue by park, honestly
items: SeaWorld Orlando — top tier earns its price; five headliners plus storm-closed afternoons concentrate demand.
SeaWorld San Diego — mid tier usually enough; Emperor and Electric Eel are the covered draws.
SeaWorld San Antonio — mid tier; Iron Rattler's queue is the one the product exists for.

sections.heading: The Legolands: nothing to buy
body: Both Legoland parks sell no line-skip product comparable to the three above. The queues that build — the Dragon, the driving schools — are managed by arrival timing and capacity, and there is no wristband that fixes a full driving-school sign-up sheet.

The honest advice is therefore scheduling, not purchasing: the Dragon at rope drop, the driving school in the first two hours, Miniland in the crowd hours, and the theater shows in the heat peak. Every Legoland page on this site builds its day around exactly that sequence.

Families who ask 'which pass should we buy at Legoland' deserve the plain answer: none exists, none is needed if you arrive at open, and the money is better spent on the photo package or the second day.

sections.heading: When to buy, park by park
body: The products are crowd insurance, so the buying rule is a crowd rule. Weekdays in the school year: never buy. Summer weekdays at the Six Flags parks: rarely. Summer weekends and holiday weeks: the mid tiers. Peak haunt-season Saturdays at Great Adventure, Great America and the SeaWorld parks: the top tiers, bought in advance, because the parks cap sales on those days.

The advance-purchase point matters more on this site than on the Disney-focused sister site: several of these products sell out on peak days, particularly top-tier FLASH Pass at the two big Six Flags parks and Quick Queue at Orlando on October Saturdays. Buying at the gate on those days can mean buying the leftover tier or nothing.
And the closing rule from the intro, repeated because it is the one readers forget: no product crosses companies. Plan each park's purchase as its own decision.

faqs.q: Does a Six Flags FLASH Pass work at Knott's or SeaWorld?
faqs.a: No — the products are company-specific and nothing crosses over. A multi-park trip is a sequence of separate decisions, and a FLASH Pass is worthless the moment you leave a Six Flags gate.

faqs.q: Is Fast Lane or Quick Queue better value?
faqs.a: Different formats for different parks: Fast Lane's wristband simplicity shines at compact Knott's, while Quick Queue's tiers match SeaWorld Orlando's concentrated headliners. Buy for the park you are actually visiting, not the brand you prefer.

faqs.q: Do these passes cover every ride?
faqs.a: No. Every product excludes some rides — usually the newest — and the exclusion list is on each park's product page. Check it before buying; discovering your target ride is excluded at the gate is the classic wasted purchase.

faqs.q: Can I buy these at the park instead of online?
faqs.a: Usually yes, but peak days sell out — particularly top-tier products on summer and haunt-season Saturdays. Online advance purchase is the safe play for any day you actually need the product.

faqs.q: What did these cost as of July 2026?
faqs.a: Ballpark ranges, honestly framed: FLASH Pass tiers from roughly $40 into the hundreds by tier and date at the Six Flags parks; Fast Lane around the mid-$100s on peak days at Knott's; Quick Queue from roughly $60 to above $100 at the SeaWorld parks. Every figure is dynamic — treat these as shapes, and the park's page as the number.
